lessons.title: What Is Python & Why Use It in Power BI?

slots.practicalActivity: Install Python and the pandas/matplotlib packages, point Power BI Desktop at that install under Options > Python scripting, then confirm the connection works by opening a new blank query, choosing Get Data > Other > Python script, and running a one-line script that creates and returns a tiny pandas DataFrame.
slots.deliverable: A working Power BI Desktop + Python install (verified in Options > Python scripting) and one .pbix containing a query loaded from a minimal Python script.

slots.practicalActivity: In any plain Python environment (VS Code, a Jupyter notebook, or the Python console), write a short script that builds a list of 5 product names and a dictionary mapping each product to a price, then loop over the list printing each product's price looked up from the dictionary.
slots.deliverable: A saved .py script demonstrating one list, one dictionary, and a loop that reads values out of the dictionary by key.

slots.practicalActivity: Build a small DataFrame from a Python dictionary by hand (products, regions, units sold, revenue), inspect it with .head(), .shape, and .dtypes, then export it to a CSV with .to_csv() and re-import it with pd.read_csv() to see the round trip.
slots.deliverable: A .py script that creates a DataFrame, writes it to a CSV file, and reloads that same CSV back into a second DataFrame.

slots.practicalActivity: Find a small real public CSV (e.g. a sample sales or weather dataset) and load it with pandas, then run and record the output of at least 6 exploratory calls: .head(), .info(), .describe(), .shape, .columns, and .dtypes, writing one sentence after each about what it told you.
slots.deliverable: A .py script loading a real CSV plus a short written log pairing each of the 6 exploratory calls with what it revealed about the dataset.

slots.practicalActivity: On your real CSV from the last slot, select 2-3 columns into their own DataFrame, filter rows using at least one combined condition with & or |, strip/lowercase a messy text column with .str methods, and check for and handle missing values with .isna() and .fillna() or .dropna().
slots.deliverable: A .py script showing a multi-column selection, a combined-condition filter, a cleaned text column, and a documented decision on how missing values were handled.

slots.practicalActivity: On the same DataFrame, deliberately duplicate a few rows and remove them with .drop_duplicates(), force at least 2 columns into the correct dtype (e.g. a price column to float, an ID column to string), and convert a date-like text column to a real datetime with pd.to_datetime() so you can pull out the year and month.
slots.deliverable: A .py script showing before/after row counts from de-duplication, corrected dtypes confirmed with .dtypes, and a datetime column with derived Year/Month columns.

slots.practicalActivity: Find a genuinely messy real-world CSV (inconsistent casing, stray whitespace, mixed date formats, some duplicate rows, a few missing values) and clean it end to end in one script: fix data types, standardize text, parse dates, drop duplicates, and handle every null column, then save the result as a new CSV.
slots.deliverable: An original 'clean_<dataset>.py' script plus the resulting cleaned CSV, with a short written list of every data-quality problem it fixed.

slots.practicalActivity: Add a calculated column to your cleaned DataFrame (e.g. Profit Margin = Profit / Revenue), use .groupby() to summarize totals by a category column, and build a small second lookup DataFrame (e.g. Region names) that you join to the main one with .merge().
slots.deliverable: A .py script with one calculated column, one groupby summary table, and one merge joining a second lookup DataFrame.

slots.practicalActivity: Using the same dataset, answer 3 original analysis questions you write yourself (e.g. 'which category has the highest average margin?', 'what's the month-over-month total?') purely with pandas groupby/merge/calculated columns, printing each answer with a short label.
slots.deliverable: A .py script answering 3 self-written analysis questions, each printed with a clear label identifying which question it answers.

lessons.title: Python vs. Power Query vs. DAX

slots.practicalActivity: Load any small dataset into Power BI Desktop, open Power Query Editor, and on the Transform tab select Run Python Script, writing a short script against the automatic `dataset` variable (e.g. filling missing values with fillna). Then write a one-paragraph decision rule for when you'd reach for Python vs. Power Query vs. DAX on a real task.
slots.deliverable: A .pbix with a working Run Python Script transform step, plus a written Python-vs-Power-Query-vs-DAX decision rule.

slots.practicalActivity: In Power BI Desktop, load the cleaned CSV built earlier in this course and recreate at least 2 of its cleaning/transform steps (one calculated column, one fillna or dropna equivalent) as a Run Python Script step in Power Query, confirming the privacy level is set to Public under Data source settings so the step can run.
slots.deliverable: A .pbix with a Python-powered Power Query transform recreating real cleaning logic from earlier in the course, with the Public privacy level confirmed in Data source settings.

slots.practicalActivity: On a report page, add a Python visual, enable script visuals, drag 2 fields into Values, and write a short Matplotlib script ending in plt.show() to render a bar or scatter chart from the auto-generated `dataset` variable.
slots.deliverable: A .pbix with one working Python visual rendering a Matplotlib chart from real fields, plus a written note on one real limitation of Python visuals (row limit, DPI, or interactivity) worth knowing before relying on it in production.

slots.practicalActivity: Without lesson guidance, take one of your earlier Power BI reports (from this course or the main Power BI course) and extend it with Python end to end: clean a new raw source with a Python script outside Power BI first, then bring the result in through a Power Query Python step or a Python visual, deciding yourself which of the two fits best and why.
slots.deliverable: An extended .pbix combining an external Python-cleaned dataset with at least one in-Power-BI Python step (Power Query script or visual), plus a short written explanation of why that particular Python integration point was chosen.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After finishing this course, a student can use Python and pandas to clean, reshape, and analyze real data outside Power BI, and knows when and how to bring that same Python logic directly into Power Query or a Python visual inside a live Power BI report.
